name: Chestnut
lede: Chestnut is the red-brown of the chestnut's shell, a word that also gave English maroon and still describes a horse's coat, a head of hair and a naturalist's chart color.

sections.title: A seed, a shell and a word
sections.body:
Chestnut is the reddish brown of the chestnut shell, and the dictionaries say so in nearly the same words: Paterson defines it as reddish-brown after the chestnut, and St Clair as a red-brown like the seed of the chestnut tree [1][2]. Latin gave English the prefix *castane-* and the rare adjective *castaneous*, "chestnut-coloured" [3]. The color word is much younger than the tree. Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary, as quoted in our library, gives 1555 as the first recorded use [4].

A second color word grew from the same nut. Paterson derives *maroon* from French *marron*, "chestnut", and adds that the French may in turn come from a Hebrew word for chestnut, which he offers as a possibility rather than a fact [5]. St Clair says maroon was originally a nut brown and is now a brownish dark red [2]. The two words therefore drifted apart: chestnut stayed the color of the shell, while maroon went darker and redder.

Which chestnut? Syme's chart, discussed below, lists "Chesnuts" and Baty's reprint glosses them as either *Castanea* or *Aesculus* [6]. Those are different trees: the sweet chestnut is *Castanea*, and the horse chestnut is *Aesculus hippocastanum* [7]. The French plate that Baty pairs with the entry shows the seed of the horse chestnut [6]. English color writing has used one word for both the edible nut and the glossy conker.

sections.title: Bark, roots and a brown lake
sections.body:
Chestnut was a color before it was a name, and trees were the source. Pastoureau lists the dyers' trades of Rome, among them the *castanearii*, who produced browns from the roots of chestnut trees [8]. In the late Middle Ages dyers made blacks and browns from the bark or roots of alder, walnut and chestnut, rich in tannin [9]. Adding an iron mordant gave grey or brown that deepened with each bath, and dyers often gave cloth a blue "foot" of woad first [9]. Pastoureau adds that these plant dyes held up poorly to sun and washing [9].

Painters borrowed the idea. The Pigment Compendium records *hypocastanum*, or chestnut brown, a transparent brown lake prepared from the horse chestnut, described by Salter in 1869 as obsolete and warmer than brown pink [10]. It also notes that species of true chestnut gave brown dyes, including one the Cherokee used, but that none is known to have been made into a pigment [10]. The same book records that Mayer (1991) used *chestnut brown* as another name for raw umber, so in a paint catalogue the words may mean a plain earth color [10].

A related tree gave yellow rather than brown. Pastoureau notes that a lake called stil de grain was made from buckthorn berries or from chestnut leaves, and gave dull slightly green yellows used for shadows and glazes [11].

sections.title: Hair, horses and cocoons
sections.body:
Chestnut is mostly a word for living things. Medieval writers described hair as a range of blonds, chestnuts, browns, reds, greys and blacks, and the lightest shades were the most admired [12]. The medieval French term *sors* meant a hair color between dark blond and light chestnut [12]. Pastoureau adds that for women in the sixteenth century new dyes and devices allowed an endless range of blond, chestnut, auburn, red and brown, each in golden, copper or grey versions [12].

Horses keep the word to this day. Paterson lists *bay* as a reddish brown or chestnut used especially of horses, *roan* as reddish-brown, chestnut or sorrel, and *strawberry roan* as a chestnut-red horse coat [13]. Finlay finds the color in silk, too: some silkworm cocoons are naturally chestnut brown, a color that comes from pigments in the sericin, and in a barkcloth skirt that he describes as chestnut-coloured [14]. Darwin, at Quasil Island, described cuttlefish ink as dark chestnut-brown [15].

None of these is a single color. A chestnut horse is closer to red than a chestnut hair, and a conker is glossier than either. The word works as a family name for the warm brown that lies between red and umber, and we treat it that way.

sections.title: Chesnut Brown in the naturalist's chart
sections.body:
In Syme's 1821 edition, entry 103 is Chesnut Brown, with examples from three kingdoms: the neck and breast of the red grouse, "Chesnuts", and Egyptian jasper [6]. Baty marks the name as one found in Werner's own lists and describes it as the characteristic brown of Werner's series, made of deep reddish brown and yellowish brown [6]. Baty's table counts it among two browns taken from the system of the Edinburgh mineralogist Robert Jameson, yet also marks it as a name found in Werner's lists, so its exact lineage is not settled [6].

Naturalists used it. Darwin's catalogue of specimens from the *Beagle* describes specimens with Werner's standards, and Baty reproduces a page where Chesnut Brown is one of the colors [16]. Baty says Syme's book sharpened Darwin's eye for animal color [16].

The swatch reconstructed from Syme's plate, #7A4B3A, is a little darker and browner than the Chestnut on this page [4]. They differ by 7 CIEDE2000 units, about the width of a neighboring name [4]. Our Chestnut is a different lineage: it descends from Ridgway's 1886 *Nomenclature of Colors*, kept in his 1912 *Color Standards* on plate II, and Ridgway's own swatch (#7D4831) is 7 units away from ours [4]. The ISCC-NBS system of 1955 files our swatch as a dark reddish orange [4].

sections.title: The swatch and the word
sections.body:
The screen color #954535 is therefore a library compromise among several charts [4]. It is redder and lighter than the swatch from Syme's Chesnut Brown [4].

Our library also files the Japanese name *kakishibu-iro*, "persimmon-juice color", at a swatch near this one [4]. It is a different plant product, not a nut, and we list it only as a secondary name [4].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a screen color within six CIEDE2000 units of this swatch covers at least five per cent of the canvas in 828 works, 3.5 per cent of the archive [17]. The color peaks in the 1400s, where 135 of 945 paintings carry it, 4.1 times the archive's rate, and in the 1450s alone 23 of 109 do [17]. That is the century of egg tempera panels, dark grounds and aged varnish, which warms everything toward brown, so some of this is age rather than paint [17].

Among painters, the Master of Alkmaar carries it in 5 of 13 works, and Dürer in 10 of 47 [17]. In countries, Tibet leads with 16 of 47 paintings and Nepal follows with 6 of 25 [17]. Inside a painting, the color is usually an accent: by the lightness-rank lens it plays that part in 85 per cent of the 738 paintings that contain it [17].

The painting where it covers the most is [[painting:commons-Q59827122|a Spanish banner of Ferdinand III]] painted in 1878, at 57 per cent [17]. Older examples include [[painting:rijks-20026322|a Sienese civic account-book panel of about 1440]] at 46 per cent, [[painting:cma-138881|a mural fragment]] of about the year 500 at 46 per cent and [[painting:nga-891|Pietro Lorenzetti's Saint Mary Magdalene]] of about 1340 at 43 per cent [17]. The first dated hit is a floor, not a first: the archive's early centuries are thin [17].

In Google Books the adjective rises fastest in the 1850s and peaks in the 1910s [18]. As always, these are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, and a color match is not a pigment test [17].

questions.q: Which color word did English take from French marron, 'chestnut'?
Why can a paint catalogue's 'chestnut brown' mean three different things?
choices: It has been a tree-bark dye, a brown lake from the horse chestnut and a synonym for raw umber
It always means a red pigment
questions.answer: It has been a tree-bark dye, a brown lake from the horse chestnut and a synonym for raw umber

questions.q: Chestnut peaks in our archive in the 1400s, so the color is purely a fifteenth-century paint.

openers: Roman dyers had a trade named for chestnut roots, the castanearii.
